title: Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Stock Price Sits 11% Below Record Highs Despite Monday's Nvidia-Driven Tech Rally - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 24, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Despite a broad surge in technology shares on Monday, Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) remains a notable distance from its peak valuation, leaving investors to weigh whether the rebound signals a genuine recovery. The stock climbed during Monday’s session as part of a wider relief rally across the technology sector, with Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) credited as a key catalyst driving renewed buying interest. Even with the gains, Microsoft shares still trade roughly 11% below their all-time high, a gap that underscores how far the stock has yet to travel to reclaim its former record levels. The tech sector has been searching for directional conviction, and Monday’s move offered at least a short-term answer, with heavyweights across the industry participating in the upswing. Nvidia’s influence over broader technology sentiment has become a recurring theme in recent months, with the chipmaker’s performance frequently setting the tone for peers across the sector. A single session of gains rarely resolves deeper questions about valuation or near-term momentum, and Microsoft’s 11% deficit to its record price keeps those questions firmly on the table. For long-term shareholders, the gap to all-time highs represents both a concern and a potential opportunity, depending on how the company’s fundamental outlook develops in coming quarters. The relief rally dynamic suggests that sentiment, rather than fresh fundamental catalysts, was the primary driver behind Monday’s advance in technology equities broadly. Microsoft’s trajectory will likely depend on whether the tech sector can sustain upward momentum beyond a single session, or whether profit-taking pulls shares back toward recent trading ranges. With the stock still meaningfully below its record, the central question facing investors heading into the final weeks of 2026 is whether Monday’s Nvidia-fueled bounce marks a turning point or simply a temporary pause in a broader consolidation. David Prior is a senior reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, covering everything from current affairs and global politics to stock market news and analysis.

Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. Microsoft (MSFT) seems to be one of the safest ways to invest in artificial intelligence (AI). The cloud and software giant posted $45.9 billion in operating income in Q1 2027. I believe that gives it considerable room to fund its next stage of growth. CEO Satya Nadella recently remarked, "We think of Copilot as the new OS for work." I like that ambition, but I also like the existing business behind it. Following the recent tech sell-off we've seen in the past few weeks, Microsoft's valuation makes that combination especially appealing. Thus, I rate MSFT stock a Buy. While "safer" is relative in tech and MSFT stock is certainly not immune to sharp pullbacks, Microsoft has built multiple ways to win as enterprises adopt AI. Rather than betting the company on a single breakthrough, it relies on cash-flowing legacy subscriptions to fund a full-stack AI ecosystem. At the infrastructure layer, Azure sells the raw computing capacity needed to train and run AI, while custom in-house silicon alongside third-party processors from Nvidia (NVDA) and AMD (AMD) reduces its reliance on any single chipmaker. If rollout in one area slows, it still has several other growth engines that can pick up the slack. In addition, I view its approach to models as quite appealing. Copilot's Auto mode automatically routes user prompts to whichever model offers the best balance of speed, capability, and cost for a given task. Similarly, Microsoft Foundry acts as an enterprise storefront offering Microsoft's proprietary models alongside rivals like OpenAI, Anthropic, and competing providers. This also includes open models. Microsoft can therefore earn from usage even when customers switch model suppliers. At its Ignite conference in November, Microsoft pushed Copilot further into practical work. The company rolled out a unified starting hub in Copilot that merges Chat for quick queries with Cowork for longer, multi-step projects, while preparing a broad rollout of Copilot Code in the coming weeks so everyday employees can build custom apps without writing code. At the same time, Microsoft rolled out governance and data tools designed to monetize the infrastructure around AI agents. Updates to Agent 365 help IT teams manage permissions and track return on investment across both Microsoft and third-party agents, while Microsoft IQ links those agents to a company's internal knowledge and workflows. As corporate AI usage scales, these supporting layers become increasingly sticky. So I think Microsoft can earn from the work happening around a model, even if it doesn't produce every winning model itself. The latest quarter shows it working already for Microsoft. In its Fiscal Q1 2027 results, Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year-over-year to $92.3 billion. Operating income increased 21% to $45.9 billion, while adjusted earnings per share (EPS) rose 18% to $4.89. Microsoft Cloud revenue climbed 30% to $63.9 billion. Azure accelerated to 48% growth, with guidance for 49%–50% constant-currency growth this quarter. That suggests customers are already using the capacity Microsoft is building. Moreover, adoption figures are encouraging. Daily Copilot users increased nearly 50% sequentially and more than fivefold year-over-year. Customers with over 50,000 Copilot seats increased more than eightfold year-over-year. Copilot revenue growth also accelerated sequentially. Foundry passed 120,000 customers, with revenue more than tripling year-over-year. Customers building agentic applications with multiple models increased fivefold year-over-year. I believe these figures suggest broader deployment, with large organizations committing to substantial usage. Volkswagen's (VWAGY) planned rollout to over 330,000 employees is one example. Microsoft also has $677 billion in remaining commercial performance obligations. This provides excellent visibility into future revenue. Operating cash flow reached $58 billion, leaving $18.6 billion of free cash flow after cash investment. So that gives it considerable internal funding for expansion. Note that enterprises are still early in putting agents into production. Yet Microsoft already supplies much of their software and identity infrastructure. Selling additional capabilities to those customers should be easier than building those relationships from scratch. Now, the recent sell-off has pushed MSFT's valuation to rather attractive levels, in my view. Today, MSFT trades at 24.59x Fiscal 2027 consensus EPS of $20.03. That falls to 20.33x Fiscal 2028 EPS of $24.23 and 16.31x Fiscal 2029 EPS of $30.20. Consensus expects roughly 16% EPS growth this year, followed by nearly 21% and 25%. I find those multiples exceptional for a business with Microsoft's recurring revenue and profitability. The estimates may also leave room for further upside. Adjusted EPS of $4.89 beat the latest $4.72 forecast. The preceding quarter delivered $4.74 against $4.24 expected. Repeated beats don't promise more, but they make me reluctant to assume consensus captures the full earnings opportunity. Azure's acceleration and wider Copilot adoption could keep driving upgrades. Delivering today's estimates alone would bring the multiple toward 16.31x by Fiscal 2029. So I don't think strong returns would rely on an aggressive rerating. Lastly, I should mention that investors are right to question returns on enormous AI spending. Microsoft's quarterly capex reached $45.2 billion, including finance leases. Competition from Amazon (AMZN) and Google (GOOGL) remains intense, and other enterprise AI platforms are also competing for customers. Infrastructure costs could pressure cloud margins, and Copilot adoption might slow. Sustaining 20%-plus earnings growth also becomes harder at Microsoft's size. However, today's cloud growth and cash generation give me more confidence in the spending. Its AI business is already producing revenue across several products. Wall Street rates MSFT a Strong Buy, based on 35 Buys and four Holds. The $632.48 average price target implies roughly 28% upside from today's price levels. Microsoft offers AI exposure without requiring one model or application to dominate. Its existing businesses fund the expansion, while Azure and Copilot already show substantial demand. Ignite adds more ways to earn from enterprise agents. At roughly 20.33x Fiscal 2028 earnings, I think the sell-off has created an attractive entry point for what could be one of the safest companies to own AI. I remain Bullish. title: Is Microsoft the Best Big Tech Stock to Buy Now? - The Globe and Mail
content: Microsoft isn't in the headlines like some of its peers are. But it is still spending big on artificial intelligence (AI). There has been a lot of talk surrounding Nvidia over the past few days, and rightfully so, amid serious allegations at the CEO level and potential company misconduct in the getting around U.S. export controls. Other companies have also been in the news such as Anthropic(NASDAQ:ANT) and its blockbuster initial public offering. However, one that has flown under the radar is Microsoft(NASDAQ:MSFT). When the market has a bearish mindset, staying under the radar as a company is normally a good idea, but a company can only keep so much of a low profile when it's the second-largest in the world by market capitalization. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » But is Microsoft a good buy today? Or should the market be worried about it too? After all, it hit a fresh all-time high just days ago. The best companies to compare Microsoft to are Alphabet(NASDAQ:GOOG)(NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Amazon(NASDAQ:AMZN). These two may not seem like great comparisons on the surface, but they are all approaching AI in a similar manner: Investing in outside companies and building out computing power. All three of these companies have significant investments in AI labs to give them exposure to the companies pioneering AI technology. While Alphabet and Amazon own a massive amount of Anthropic (about 30% combined), Microsoft owns nearly the same amount of OpenAI, its primary competitor. While OpenAI isn't public yet, it will likely become so in the near future, and is likely keeping an eye on how successful Anthropic is on the public markets. So, Microsoft's payday for its OpenAI investment will need to wait, which may not be a bad thing. The other area these three compete heavily in is cloud computing. AI firms don't have the resources to build out an extensive data center network to power their workloads. So, they choose to rent it from providers like Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Google Cloud. All three companies have seen their backlog explode from massive AI computing demand, and the backlog totals are in the hundreds of billions for each company. As a result, each company is spending heavily to build out its computing capacity. However, Microsoft is being less aggressive, which the market respects. This year, both Amazon and Alphabet plan to spend at least $200 billion on data center capital expenditures. Microsoft only plans to spend $170 billion. While this may sound like it's falling behind, the reality is that Microsoft isn't stretching itself thin. Microsoft has maintained strong free cash flow, meaning that it's still sending cash to the bottom line. Amazon and Alphabet have dipped into negative territory, meaning they are either burning through cash reserves to fund operations or taking out loans. Both of these two activities aren't favorable in the market's eyes. This could lead to Microsoft being viewed more favorably, but it could cost it some market share in the end if it isn't aggressive enough. The market normally takes a short-term view for situations like this, which is why Microsoft's stock is viewed favorably. But does that make it a smart buy now? Microsoft is already in its fiscal 2027, ending June 30. So comparing forward earnings price tags is a bit difficult to its peers. But at 25 times forward earnings, Microsoft is neither expensive nor cheap. Amazon is nearly in line with Microsoft's valuation at 24.5 times fiscal 2027 earnings estimates, but Alphabet is far cheaper at 18 times next year's earnings. That's a big mismatch, and could point to Alphabet being a smarter buy than Microsoft, especially if it can steal some of its cloud computing market share. Microsoft is staying conservative in its spending. We'll see if it costs them, but as of right now, I'd say Microsoft is an OK stock to buy. It will likely beat the market, but won't do it by much due to its current price tag. title: Microsoft Stock Falls 7% in a Month as 24-Hour Outage Triggers "Code Red" - Coinpaper
content: Microsoft declares an internal Code Red after a nearly 24-hour global outage exposes infrastructure flaws, while MSFT stock struggles below $500. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) has declared an internal "Code Red" initiative following a nearly 24-hour global service outage that exposed significant weaknesses in its engineering infrastructure and emergency response procedures. The development comes as Microsoft stock trades around $493, down approximately 7.5% from its October 26 closing price of $532.60 and more than 11% from its November closing high of $555.80. The software giant faces renewed scrutiny over its operational reliability amid a broader Big Tech stock selloff and growing investor concerns about artificial intelligence infrastructure spending. According to internal company documents reviewed by Reuters, Microsoft has made infrastructure reliability its highest engineering priority following the November 12–13 disruption. The global Microsoft 365 outage affected Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and Copilot, disrupting communications across businesses, governments and financial institutions. Microsoft attributed the incident to an undetected scalability defect introduced into Windows in July. The company ruled out both malicious cyber activity and AI agents as causes. The internal review also exposed shortcomings in how engineering teams coordinated recovery efforts. Microsoft now intends to restore global services within one hour during future incidents, improve traffic management and introduce AI-assisted diagnostic tools. The incident arrives at a critical moment for Microsoft's cloud and artificial intelligence expansion. According to its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results, Microsoft generated $92.3 billion in quarterly revenue, representing 19% annual growth. Net income increased 32% to $36.6 billion. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, up 30% year over year, while Azure revenue increased 48%. Reported Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue grew 17%. Most ESG ratings tell you how well a company reports. Very few tell you whether the business is actually efficient. $MSFT is the cleanest example I know of the gap. Its own figures run from 13 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent in 2020 to 20 million in 2025, against a pledge to be carbon negative by 2030. Energy use, by its own account, has grown far faster than revenue. None of that makes Microsoft a bad company. It is one of the best-run businesses in the world. It makes it a company where a sustainability rating and operational efficiency are answering two different questions. Back in 2021 we started checking what ESG funds actually held. A number held oil majors. Others held the technology companies building energy-hungry AI infrastructure. These were not obscure funds, and they carried strong ratings. Eco-efficiency asks how much energy and material a company consumes to earn each dollar of return. It draws on emissions, energy and resource intensity, reported operational data, and thermodynamic return on invested capital, which puts return against the energy and resources consumed to produce it. A business that needs less energy and material to earn a dollar is usually better run. It wastes less, it is less exposed when input costs move, and it has more room when conditions turn. That makes it a capital preservation measure rather than a moral one. Buying a stock because it carries a sustainability label, at any price, is not a plan. title: Toto Wolff Backs Human Instinct Over Data As Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Powers Mercedes F1's AI Race Machine - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 21, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis When ten million simulations point one way and the driver says another, Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team Principal Toto Wolff has a clear answer: trust the human. Wolff and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Commercial Business CEO Judson Althoff spoke with Yahoo Finance on November 20, outlining the scope of artificial intelligence now embedded across the Mercedes F1 operation. The partnership spans car design, factory workflows, personnel management, and race-day strategy, representing one of the most compute-intensive deployments in professional motorsport. Althoff described a layered infrastructure in which analysts based in the United Kingdom, engineers in the pit garage, and the driver in the cockpit must all align within millisecond windows during a race. The Singapore Grand Prix offered a vivid illustration, with Wolff and his team working through rapid-fire calculations about precisely when driver Kimi should make a passing move under live race conditions. More than 10 million race-day simulations run behind that kind of decision, feeding a compute fabric that Althoff said most people outside the sport would struggle to fully appreciate in terms of sheer pressure and intensity. Yet for all that processing power, the most persistent tension inside the team is not a technical one — it is the long-running friction between what sensors record and what a driver physically feels. Wolff, who positions himself as a mediator between the data-driven engineering culture and the instinct-driven world of the driver, described the conflict as predating the current wave of AI entirely. “It was always a theme, even before AI, that the engineer would say, this is what the car does and the driver say, no, no, it doesn’t do that,” Wolff said, describing a divide that better algorithms have not closed. His resolution to that conflict carries weight given Mercedes’ investment in machine intelligence: when data and human judgment diverge, the driver wins. “I’m siding with the human because the human needs to drive the car and the human needs to feel the confidence in driving it,” Wolff said, adding that driver preference overrides what the numbers might identify as the faster setup. Wolff framed the driver as the team’s single most valuable sensor, describing the person behind the wheel as “the one that sits in the car” — and the most expensive instrument Mercedes deploys. The stance raises a broader question for organizations racing to automate decision-making: at what point does accumulated data become less reliable than embodied human experience operating under extreme conditions. For Mercedes, at least at race speed, that threshold has already been defined — no simulation, however vast, outranks the judgment of the driver holding the wheel.
